title: Sweep Picking
goal: Sweep clean, separated arpeggios from two strings to six, and link them through minor-key progressions so they sound like a solo.
assumes: You can alternate-pick single notes evenly at sixteenths around 80 BPM (Alternate Picking through its Intermediate Level covers this) and you can hammer on and pull off cleanly. You don't need any sweeping yet, and you can start at whichever Level suits you.

skills: Even alternate picking at sixteenths, 80 BPM

orderRationale: Three Levels, each open from the start. Beginner is one shape, clean: the mute from the first Exercise, because it separates a sweep from a strummed chord and bad habits here are hard to undo, then the turnaround on three strings where it's cheapest to learn. Intermediate is built around linking, which the owner asked for as the backbone and which I agree with. Qualities come first because a link needs a named chord to go to, and the major V isn't a shape you can skip. The link is taught as its own skill on three strings before any bigger shape, slowly and in isolation, then in chains, and only then with four and five strings, because a long shape makes a bad link worse. Five-string shapes still get their own Step before being linked. The harmonic-minor V comes after chains so it is the one new thing. Advanced adds six strings, wide shifts and neoclassical sequences. Six strings are there because players want them; they add reach and discipline more than music, so they are one Step and not the point of the Level. Two choices here go against the examples I was given. A major ii-V-I has no Step of its own: this Path is minor-key, so the minor ii°-V-i takes its place. And chains change chord once a bar, because Jam's grid is one chord to a bar, where fast playing in this style often changes every two beats. That is a limit of the backing today, not a teaching choice. The progressions are common vocabulary and every line is written for this Path: nothing is transcribed from a song or copied from a course.
gradingLimits: Grading stops being trustworthy at about 150 ms between notes: sixteenths at 100 BPM, eighth triplets at 133, sextuplets at 66. Rungs faster than that are self-checked, whatever they look like, and the card says where grading stops. That line is a cautious policy, not a measurement. No test anywhere covers swept notes, whose attacks are softer than picked ones and whose notes can ring on neighbouring strings, and even the graded rungs are provisional until there has been a real-guitar test. Links add a risk of their own: the note after a slide counts as missed if it isn't heard, so bars on sliding shapes are lower. In practice: Beginner is almost all graded. In Intermediate, the sixteenth-note shapes stop at 100 BPM and triplet shapes at 130, and the sextuplet pickup at 65. In Advanced most of what makes the playing hard can't be graded: sextuplet runs stop at 65 BPM, six-string shapes in sixteenths stop at 100. Sound never tells us the two things that matter most here, muting and pick path, and the Exercises say so.

steps.title: Two strings, one stroke, and the mute
steps.goal: One continuous push of the pick through two strings, with two separate notes and nothing ringing.
steps.why: A sweep is one motion that plays several notes, which is why it is not alternate picking done faster. The smallest sweep is two strings, and it contains the whole technique: push through the first string, let the pick come to rest on the next, then push on. It also contains the whole problem: if the first note keeps ringing, you get a chord. Learn the mute now, while there are only two notes to keep apart.
howTo: Use a single push from the arm, with the wrist quiet. Think of a slow, heavy push rather than two small picks. The pick comes to rest on the next string between notes.
Fretting hand: as soon as the next note sounds, release the pressure on the last note without leaving the string. That is the left-hand mute, and it does most of the work.
Picking hand: keep the side of your palm on the lower strings, moving across with the sweep, so everything behind the pick stays silent.
Go slowly enough to hear two distinct notes. If you can't, it is too fast or a note is still ringing.
steps.payoff: A two-string lick you can play at any slow tempo and hear each note clearly, and a short pentatonic phrase that uses it.

exercises.title: Down through two strings
exercises.purpose: The motion on its own: down through the B and E strings, then stop.
howTo: Push through the B string and let the pick rest on the E string, then push through that. Stop for the rest and start again from above the B string.
exercises.coachLine: I can time the two notes and hear whether both were there. Listening for a ring between them is your job.

exercises.title: Roll one finger across three strings
exercises.purpose: Fret 5 on three strings with one finger: the fingertip rolls so only the current note sounds. This is the fretting skill behind every barred sweep shape.
howTo: First finger across G, B and E at fret 5. Going up the strings, roll the fingertip so the finger leaves the last string as the next one sounds. Coming back, roll the other way.
Play it very slowly first with no click, and listen for two notes sounding together.

steps.title: Three strings, each way
steps.goal: A clean one-way triad on the top three strings, at a tempo where each note can be told apart.
steps.why: Three strings is the first time a sweep sounds like one: three notes of a chord in one gesture. Keep it one-way for now so that all the attention is on the push and the mute, and so that you learn the shape as music rather than as a move.
howTo: Same single push, now through three strings. Keep the pick rest going: the pick lands on each string, then falls through it.
The Am shape at fret 14 uses first finger on the top string, second on the B string, third on the G string. Lift each finger's pressure as soon as the next note sounds.
Rest between sweeps. The rest is also a check: does anything keep ringing?
steps.payoff: You hear an actual arpeggio come out of one stroke, and you can play Am, F, C and G that way.

steps.title: Changing direction: the turnaround
steps.goal: Turn the sweep round at the top with a hammer and a pull, so it keeps flowing with no extra pick stroke.
steps.why: A sweep that goes one way is a trick. A sweep that goes up and comes back is a line, and the turn is where it usually falls apart: the pick is going down when the music needs it to come back. A hammer and a pull on the top string give the pick time to change direction without a stroke being heard. Learn it now on three strings, where there is little else to get wrong.
howTo: After the top string's push, the next note is a hammer-on, so the pick has nothing to do. Use that moment to turn it round.
The pull-off back is the last note before the upward push begins. Keep the pull clean: pull slightly sideways, off the string, and do not just lift.
Start with C major: its reach on the top string is three frets. The minor shapes reach five, and they come next.
steps.payoff: A triad that loops without a seam, with the turn inaudible, at a tempo you can sing along with.

exercises.title: C major, the short reach
exercises.purpose: The whole loop with the shortest top-string reach. G, C, E, then hammer to G and back.
howTo: Triplets. The first note of the loop after the first pass is an upstroke: the sweep comes back through it and turns, so you are never starting over.
exercises.coachLine: I'll say whether the notes were C major and how even they were. A quiet hammer does not count against you.

steps.title: Major, minor, then diminished
steps.goal: Play major, minor and diminished shapes on three strings, and hear exactly which note changes between them.
steps.why: A shape you can name is a shape you can use. Major and minor differ by one fret on one string, and that is the best ear training you can get on a guitar. Diminished comes last because it sounds tense and wants to go somewhere; it is what makes a sweep sound like the fast, dramatic thing you came to this Path for.
howTo: Name the notes out loud as you practise, at least once. The spelled notes on each Exercise are there for that.
Moving between inversions, shift during the last note of the bar, and arrive on the first finger of the new shape.
Diminished seventh shapes repeat every three frets with the same four notes. You only have to learn it once.
steps.payoff: You can hear a C major become C minor under your own fingers, and an A minor sweep resolving from its diminished neighbour sounds like the real thing.

steps.title: The link: two shapes
steps.goal: Get from one arpeggio into the next with no gap and no extra pick stroke, slowly enough to hear the join.
steps.why: Linked arpeggios are what make a sweep sound like a solo and not an exercise, and the link is a separate skill from either shape. Almost everyone practises the shapes and hopes the join comes along. It doesn't: the join is where the pick stops, the hand arrives late and a note gets lost. So here it gets practised alone, as slowly as you like, with nothing else to think about.
howTo: A link is one small move of the fretting hand. On the top or bottom string, step from the last note of the old shape to the nearest note of the new one with a hammer, a pull or a slide. The pick does nothing at that moment.
Choose the nearest note of the new chord, not the root. Good links barely move the hand, which is why the shapes here may look unfamiliar.
Look ahead. Know the note you are stepping to before you play the note you are stepping from.
Keep muting through the change: the last note of the old shape stops as the new one sounds.
steps.payoff: You hear one line carry on across a chord change, and a chord change that happens under your fingers instead of between two shapes.

exercises.title: Just the link
exercises.purpose: Four notes in half notes: the last two of one shape, the first two of the next. There is nothing to do but hear the chord change on one small move.
howTo: Bar 1 is the end of the old shape, bar 2 the start of the new one. The first note of bar 2 is not picked: hammer, pull or slide to it, and only then cross to the next string.
Say the chord names. If you can't tell which chord you're on, slow down until you can.
exercises.coachLine: Very slow on purpose. I can check the notes against each chord after the take.

steps.title: Chains of links
steps.goal: Link four chords in a row on three strings, without stopping, in any minor key.
steps.why: Once two shapes link, the question becomes how long you can keep it going. A four-chord chain is the unit of real playing, and the minor-key loops here are the most common things you will be asked to sweep over. The moves are small, so the hard part is keeping your place: you should know which chord is next without counting.
howTo: Learn the chords by ear first. Play the progression's roots, once through, on the low strings.
Each chord's shape starts as near as it can to the last one. Don't reach for the shape you know best: reach for the nearest one.
If a link trips you, go back to two shapes and repeat that one link. Don't push through it.
steps.payoff: A four-chord minor progression comes out of one unbroken sweep, in whichever key you land on today.

exercises.title: One pass per chord

howTo: Three notes a bar. Sing the progression's top notes if you can: they make a tune.
exercises.coachLine: Four links per round. I can check notes and evenness at these tempos.

steps.title: Four strings
steps.goal: Add the D string without losing the separation you built on three.
steps.why: Four strings is enough for a full-sounding chord and short enough to keep clean. The palm mute now has to travel with the pick, and the fretting hand keeps releasing each note in turn.
The bottom note is played once: you arrive on it with the upward push and leave it with a downstroke on the next string. Keep that change small.
steps.payoff: A sweep that sounds like a real chord being spelled out, at a tempo you can sing, in four shapes.

steps.title: Five strings: the root positions
steps.goal: Own the two common five-string shapes with the root on the A string, in minor and major.
steps.why: Five strings is the big sweep, the sound people mean when they say the word. There are few shapes to learn: minor from the A string, major from the A string, and the two moved around. Everything else on the fretboard is one of those at a different fret, which is why you learn only these.

steps.title: Minor keys and the V chord
steps.goal: Link through the harmonic-minor movement: the major V chord pulling back to i.
steps.why: A natural-minor loop goes round forever and never needs to resolve. The major V chord is what changes that: its G# sits a half step under A and pulls back to it, and that pull is the dark, dramatic sound of metal and neoclassical playing. These progressions are shared vocabulary, and the thing to learn is the half-step move: it is the link you will come to love.
howTo: E major in A minor contains G#, a note A minor doesn't have. Find it in the shape. It is where the sound comes from.
Aim for the G# to A step at the resolution, and hear it before you play it.
Bdim to E to Am is the minor two-five-one. It is the same pull with one more chord of warning.
steps.payoff: You hear a chord pull back to the minor at the end of a sweep, and a progression sounds like it's going somewhere.

steps.title: Sweeps inside phrases
steps.goal: Use a sweep as part of a line that goes somewhere, starting and ending in a scale or on a held note.
steps.why: Nobody wants to hear ten bars of arpeggio. What makes a sweep sound exciting is what comes either side of it: a line that arrives by sweep, then sings; a run that shoots up to a held bend. This Step turns the shapes into something you could actually play in a solo.
howTo: The held note after a sweep matters more than the sweep. Give it time and a little vibrato.
Change technique cleanly. When a sweep ends, you go straight back to normal picking, with no moment of confusion in the hand.

steps.goal: Play sweeps that follow Am, F, C, G over a band, from three strings up to five, and one chorus you put together yourself.

howTo: Keep the volume honest: if the band is covering your mistakes, turn it down until they show.

steps.title: Six strings
steps.goal: Own a clean six-string sweep from the low E, minor and major, and link passes across all six.
steps.why: Six strings is the longest push you can make, and it is a real physical challenge, since the arm travels the whole width of the neck and every string behind the pick has to stay quiet. It adds less new music than the step from three to five did. Come to it for the sound and for the discipline: a clean six-string sweep shows up any weakness in your muting at once.
howTo: The arm does this. The wrist stays quiet, and the forearm carries the pick from the low E to the high E in one long push.
Muting is the whole game: palm on what's behind the pick, the fretting fingers rolling off what's in front of it. Low strings ring loudest, so check them first.
Grading on these is limited: only the slowest rungs are graded, and even those have never been tried on a real guitar.
steps.payoff: A sweep from the lowest note on the guitar to near the highest, with every note separate.

exercises.title: Minor, from the low E

howTo: Fourteen sixteenths and a rest. Hammer on the low E and on the top string. Up to 100 BPM it can be graded, and above that it's your own ear.
exercises.coachLine: Graded only to 100 BPM. Trust a recording above that: long sweeps are where I'm least sure of myself.

steps.title: Wide shapes and fast shifts
steps.goal: Jump between shapes far apart on the neck, and play sweeps fast enough that grading no longer applies.
steps.why: Everything until now has moved a fret or two. Sometimes a line needs an octave jump, and that's a throw of the whole arm that has to land exactly. This is also where speed comes in, so it's where the app can't help much: you'll be working by recording and by ear, as players always have.
howTo: Look at the landing spot before you leave. The hand follows the eye.
A shift is one fast movement and then stillness. Land early and let the note come to you.
Fast rungs are self-checked. Record yourself and slow the recording down: nothing is more honest than that.
steps.payoff: A line that jumps the neck, and a burst of sweep at a speed you couldn't have played a month ago.

exercises.title: The octave jump

howTo: Two loops, then jump. The first note after the jump is what tells you if you got there.
exercises.coachLine: A note missing after the jump is the thing to listen for. I can usually hear whether that note arrived.

steps.title: Neoclassical sequences
steps.goal: Play the moves that give this style its sound: diminished shapes climbing in minor thirds, and triads walking up the harmonic minor scale.
steps.why: Baroque-flavoured metal comes from a few harmonic ideas played very fast: the major V, the diminished seventh on its leading tone, and triads walked in sequence. You've met the first two. A sequence adds the sense of a long line unfolding, and a diminished chord that moves three frets at a time is the most fun you can have with one shape.
howTo: A diminished seventh is the same four notes every three frets. So G#dim7, Bdim7, Ddim7 and Fdim7 are one sound in four places.
In a sequence, hear each bar as the next step of one melody. The top notes usually tell the tale.
These are original lines in a shared style, and meant as starting points: write your own as soon as you can.
steps.payoff: The unmistakable sound of a neoclassical run, in lines you can change and call your own.

exercises.coachLine: I can check the notes after the take. It sounds grand, I hope, but that part is for you to judge.

exercises.title: Triads up the harmonic minor
exercises.purpose: The chords of the harmonic minor, walking up the neck a step at a time. It's a sequence: a long line that unfolds, and it finishes high on the V. It leaves out the third degree, whose augmented chord doesn't suit this style.
howTo: One chord a bar, and each shape sits higher than the last. Note the two chords the harmonic minor changes: E major and G# diminished. This one runs once through and stops.
exercises.coachLine: Eight bars is long. If you get lost, the chord names on the tab are the way back in.

steps.title: A heavy band, a long line
steps.goal: Play linked five- and six-string sweeps over a band in a minor key, and make your own chorus from them.
steps.why: It's the point of the whole Level. A loud band sits on the low strings and leaves the top of the neck to you, so a long sweep cuts through. It also hides your mistakes, which is why a recording matters even more here than before.
howTo: Turn the band down until your mistakes show.
Use direct input or headphones for any graded take: a microphone hears the band as well, and that hasn't been tested.
Grading covers the slower rungs only. Above them you're on your own, with your ears and a recording.
steps.payoff: You play a long, linked, minor-key arpeggio line over a band.

levels.summary: The backbone of this Path. Name the shapes, learn the link between two of them, then chain them through minor-key progressions on three, four and five strings.
